title: Understanding Addiction
hook: Addiction isn't a lack of willpower or a moral failing — it's a treatable medical condition that changes how the brain works. And like other chronic illnesses, it responds to treatment.
key_points: Addiction is a chronic, treatable brain disease, not a character flaw.
Repeated substance use changes brain circuits for reward, stress, and self-control.
Effective treatment often combines medication with behavioral therapy.
Relapse is common and signals treatment should resume or adjust, not that it failed.
Recovery is possible; reaching out for help is a strength, not a weakness.
content_html: When someone struggles with addiction, it's easy to chalk it up to weak willpower or bad choices. The science tells a different story: addiction is a chronic medical condition in which substances hijack the brain's circuits for reward, motivation, and self-control — and, importantly, it can be treated.
extra_html: The National Institute on Drug Abuse explains that repeated use of drugs or alcohol changes how the brain functions, which is why stopping can be so hard even when someone genuinely wants to. Treating it like a moral failing tends to push people away from the help that works. Effective treatment usually combines medication, where appropriate, with behavioral therapies and ongoing support, and is tailored to the person. Recovery is a process rather than a single event, and relapse — as with other chronic illnesses like diabetes or high blood pressure — is common and means treatment should be resumed or adjusted, not abandoned. Reaching out to a clinician or a service like SAMHSA's national helpline is a practical first step.

source.name: U.S. National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA)

related.title: Alcohol and Your Health
related.hook: There's no amount of alcohol proven to be good for you — but there's a meaningful difference between a glass with dinner and patterns that quietly raise your risk of cancer, liver disease, and more.

related.title: Quitting Smoking
related.hook: Your body starts repairing itself within hours of your last cigarette. Quitting is hard and relapse is common — but the right support roughly doubles your odds of success.

related.title: What Mental Health Really Means
related.hook: Mental health isn't just the absence of illness — it's being able to cope with life's stresses, work, learn, and contribute. Everyone has it, and it can be cared for.

related.title: An Experimental Vaccine Against Fentanyl Overdose
related.hook: Scripps researchers are testing a vaccine that trains the immune system to grab fentanyl in the bloodstream before it reaches the brain — and to recognize a broad range of its deadliest variants.

related.title: Teen Cannabis Use and Serious Mental Illness
related.hook: A study of more than 463,000 adolescents tied teen cannabis use to roughly double the risk of serious mental illness — and the use usually came first.

choices.text: A chronic, treatable medical condition affecting the brain

flashcards.explanation_html: NIDA describes addiction as a chronic but treatable disease in which repeated substance use alters brain circuits — not a moral failing.

flashcards.prompt: What does relapse during recovery indicate?
flashcards.back_html: Relapse is common in chronic conditions and signals that treatment needs to resume or be adjusted — not that treatment failed or recovery is impossible.
